Isaiah 1:11: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the LORD."
Hosea 6:6, quoted by Jesus in Matthew 9:13: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."

Many scholars read Isaiah 66:3 as a word to Isaiah's own time against worship mixed with idolatry or hypocrisy, not as a prophecy about the first century. Others translate the verse differently, as listing both proper offerings and pagan practices done by the same people.
If a temple were rebuilt in Jerusalem today, what would it mean on this reading?
It would have no place in fulfilling New Testament prophecy. For Christians, sacrifice for sin was finished at the cross, and God's temple is his people.

On the fulfilled reading, a temple built now would not be the temple of Matthew 24, 2 Thessalonians 2 or Revelation 11. Those texts spoke of the building standing in the first century. Hebrews teaches that Christ "has appeared once for all" to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26). So Christians believe no new animal sacrifice can add to his work (Hebrews 10:18). A new temple would show only that its builders do not yet see Jesus as the Messiah, which is the same disagreement that existed in the first century. This should lead Christians to prayer and gentle witness, not to excitement about a countdown. Paul longed for his own people to be saved (Romans 10:1). He also warned Gentile believers against pride (Romans 11:18-20).
Romans 10:1: "My heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved."
In AD 363 Emperor Julian tried to rebuild the temple to disprove Christianity; the work stopped after fires broke out (Ammianus Marcellinus, History 23.1.2-3).

Dispensationalists would see a rebuilt temple as an important prophetic event, since it would make possible the events of Daniel 9:27 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4. They also stress love for the Jewish people. Many other Christians, with this reading, see no prophetic weight in such a building.
What is the "abomination of desolation" that Jesus mentions in Matthew 24:15?
It is Daniel's phrase for a sacrilege in God's house that leads to its ruin. Jesus said his own hearers would see it.

The phrase comes from Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11. In the Old Testament an "abomination" is false worship or the defiling of true worship (Deuteronomy 7:25; Deuteronomy 17:1). "Desolation" means the place is left empty and ruined. So the phrase means a defiling act that brings the sanctuary to ruin. Jesus told his disciples, "when you see" it, and then he said that "this generation" would not pass before all these things happened (Matthew 24:15, 34). On the fulfilled reading, the event belongs to the years before AD 70, when the temple in Jerusalem was still standing. Daniel 9:26 had already joined the phrase to the destruction of "the city and the sanctuary" after the Messiah is "cut off". Jesus is pointing his hearers to that ruin.
Daniel 9:26-27 places the desolation after the Messiah is "cut off" and links it to the ruin of the city and the sanctuary.
1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the same phrase for the pagan altar set up by Antiochus IV in December 167 BC, so first-century Jews knew the words well.

Dispensational futurists see a double reference: Antiochus was a preview, and the full fulfilment comes when a future Antichrist defiles a rebuilt temple in the middle of a seven-year tribulation. Many amillennial and historic premillennial scholars accept AD 70 as the main fulfilment but also see a pattern that may recur at the end.
Does Matthew 24:15 require a rebuilt temple in our future?
On the fulfilled reading, no. The "holy place" Jesus meant was the temple his disciples were looking at, which stood until AD 70.

The whole discourse begins with the temple in front of the disciples. Jesus said of those buildings, "not one stone here will be left on another" (Matthew 24:1-2). The disciples then asked when "these things" would happen (Matthew 24:3). Read in that setting, the "holy place" of verse 15 is the same temple. Nothing in the chapter speaks of a second building or a gap of many centuries. Jesus also tied every item to "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). So this reading says a future temple must be brought into the text from elsewhere. It is not found in the text itself. The fulfilled reading adds that Hebrews calls the earthly sanctuary a "copy and shadow" which was ready to vanish (Hebrews 8:5, 13).
Matthew 24:1-3 moves straight from the standing temple to the question "when will these things be?"
The Herodian temple was burned in August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7). No later temple has been built on the site.

Futurists point to 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2, which they read as a future temple. They argue that Jesus' words were only partly fulfilled in AD 70 and await a final completion. Some premillennial scholars expect a temple without holding a strict seven-year timetable.
What did Antiochus IV Epiphanes do, and why does it matter for Matthew 24?
In 167 BC he set up a pagan altar on God's altar and forced Jews to break the law. Jews of Jesus' day saw this as the classic "abomination".

Antiochus IV ruled the Seleucid empire. In December 167 BC (15 Kislev), his officials set up an "abomination of desolation" on the altar of burnt offering. Ten days later pagan sacrifice was offered there (1 Maccabees 1:54, 59). He banned circumcision and Sabbath keeping. Many who refused were killed (1 Maccabees 1:60-63). Judas Maccabeus cleansed the temple in December 164 BC, which Hanukkah remembers (1 Maccabees 4:52-59; John 10:22). Daniel 11:31 is widely read as foretelling this. When Jesus used the same phrase, his hearers would think of a pagan power defiling the sanctuary. The fulfilled reading says Jesus was warning that a similar event would come in their own lifetime, but this time it would end in the temple's total ruin.
Some summaries date the altar to 168 BC. 1 Maccabees 1:54 gives the year 145 of the Seleucid era, which is December 167 BC.
Josephus says Antiochus forced the Jews to leave their infants uncircumcised and to offer swine on the altar (Jewish War 1.1.2).

Most scholars of every view agree that Daniel 11:31 points to Antiochus. Futurists add that Daniel 11:36-45 shifts to a later king. They also note that Jesus spoke of the abomination as still to come, so Antiochus cannot be its only fulfilment. Critical scholars date Daniel to the time of Antiochus.
How does Luke 21:20 help us understand Matthew 24:15?
Where Matthew says "abomination of desolation", Luke says "Jerusalem surrounded by armies". Both give the same signal to flee from Judea.

Matthew 24:15-16, Mark 13:14 and Luke 21:20-21 sit at the same point in the same discourse. Each is followed by the same command: "let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains". Luke, writing for Gentile readers, explains the Hebrew phrase in plain terms. The desolation is near when armies surround Jerusalem. On the fulfilled reading, this ties the sign to the Roman war of AD 66-70. The armies arrive, the desolation follows, and the disciples must leave at once. Luke also adds that Jerusalem would be "trodden down by the Gentiles" and its people led away captive (Luke 21:24). That happened in AD 70. Comparing the three Gospels side by side lets Scripture explain Scripture.
Matthew 24:16, Mark 13:14 and Luke 21:21 all give the identical command to flee to the mountains.
Cestius Gallus surrounded Jerusalem in November AD 66. Titus set up a full siege in spring AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19; 5.1-2).

Many futurists accept that Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70 but argue that Matthew 24:15 describes a later event. Others say Luke keeps both levels in view, moving to the end of the age at Luke 21:25. Some evangelical scholars hold that Luke shows the AD 70 meaning, while Matthew's wording leaves room for a later echo.
Do Matthew and Luke describe two different events, one past and one future?
The fulfilled reading says no. The setting, the question, the warning and the time limit are the same in all three Gospels.

Some dispensational writers, such as Arno Gaebelein, taught that Luke records the fall of Jerusalem under Titus while Matthew 24 skips it and describes a future tribulation. The fulfilled reading answers that the three accounts share the same setting on the Mount of Olives, the same question from the disciples, and the same command to flee from Judea. They also share the same time limit: "this generation will not pass away" (Matthew 24:34; Mark 13:30; Luke 21:32). If the time limit is the same, the events cannot be separated by thousands of years. Matthew wrote for Jewish readers and kept Daniel's words. Luke wrote for Gentiles and explained them. The difference is in the wording, not in the event.
The time statement is almost identical in Matthew 24:34, Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32.
Matthew 24:20 adds "nor on a Sabbath", a detail that suits Jewish readers in first-century Judea.

Futurists answer that Matthew and Mark do not mention armies, and that Matthew 24:21 speaks of unequalled distress, which they think fits the end. Some say Luke 21:24 shows a long gap ("the times of the Gentiles") between AD 70 and the final signs. Historic premillennial writers often see a near and a far fulfilment woven together.
Did first-century Jews expect Daniel's abomination to happen in their own day?
Yes. When Emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordered his statue placed in the temple about AD 40, many Jews feared Daniel's words were being fulfilled.

Around AD 39-40 the Emperor Gaius, called Caligula, ordered the governor Petronius to set up a statue of himself in the Jerusalem temple. Thousands of Jews pleaded with Petronius and said they would die first. Petronius delayed. Caligula was murdered in January AD 41, and the plan died with him (Philo, Embassy to Gaius 188-337; Josephus, Antiquities 18.8.2-9; Tacitus, Histories 5.9). This crisis shows that Jews of that time thought Daniel's warning could come true in their generation. Mark 13:14 was written soon after. The fulfilled reading says the danger was only delayed. What Caligula failed to do in AD 40, the Roman legions did in AD 70, when they brought their standards into the temple court.
Tacitus records that the Jews took up arms rather than let Caligula's statue be set up (Histories 5.9).
Philo led a delegation to Caligula in Rome about AD 40 and wrote an account of it.

Most scholars of all views accept these historical details. Some futurists see the Caligula crisis as one more "preview" that shows how a future ruler might act. Some critical scholars think Mark 13 was shaped by the Caligula crisis.
Did Josephus think Daniel's prophecy was fulfilled in the Roman war?
Yes. Josephus wrote that Daniel foresaw Roman rule and that Jerusalem would be taken and the temple laid waste.

Josephus was a Jewish priest and general who later lived under Roman patronage. In Antiquities 10.11.7 (10.276) he says Daniel wrote about the Roman government and that Jerusalem would be taken and the temple made desolate. He also tells of an old saying that the city would fall when Jews themselves defiled the temple. He saw this fulfilled in the crimes of the Zealots inside the temple courts in 67-68 (Jewish War 4.6.3; 6.2.1). So a Jewish writer who was not a Christian linked Daniel to the events of AD 66-70. On the fulfilled reading, this shows that the AD 70 interpretation is not a later Christian invention. It fits how Jews read Daniel at the time.
Antiquities 10.11.7: Daniel "also wrote concerning the Roman government" and its taking of Jerusalem.
Jewish War 6.2.1: Josephus urges the rebels to see that ancient prophecies about the city's fall were being fulfilled.

Futurists reply that Josephus was not inspired and that his reading of Daniel does not settle what Jesus meant. They note that Josephus also hailed Vespasian as the ruler foretold in Jewish oracles (Jewish War 6.5.4), which shows his views served his Roman patrons.
Could the Zealots' actions in the temple be the abomination?
Many think so. In 67-68 the Zealots turned the temple into a fortress, shed blood in its courts and made a mock high priest.

The Zealots were Jewish nationalists who fought Roman rule. One of Jesus' apostles had been called "Simon the Zealot" (Luke 6:15). During the revolt, Zealot groups seized the temple. Josephus says they made the holy place a stronghold, let men with blood on their hands walk inside, and killed people in the courts (Jewish War 4.3.7). In the winter of 67-68 they chose a new high priest by lot. He was Phannias (Phanni), a country man who did not even understand the office (Jewish War 4.3.8). The former high priest Ananus wept and said he wished he had died before seeing God's house so defiled (Jewish War 4.3.10). This reading fits the idea of defilement "by Jewish hands", which Josephus saw in an old prophecy.
Jewish War 4.3.8: Phannias is chosen by lot and dressed in the high priest's robes.
Jewish War 4.3.10: Ananus mourns that the holy places are "crowded with the feet of murderers".

Some scholars think the Zealot occupation came too late to serve as a signal to flee, since by then escape was hard. Others prefer the Roman armies, following Luke 21:20. Futurists say none of these acts fully matches an abomination set up "in the holy place" by one ruler who claims to be God.
What happened when the Idumeans entered Jerusalem, and why did Josephus see it as a turning point?
The Idumeans, let in by the Zealots in a storm, killed thousands in the temple courts and murdered the former high priest Ananus. Josephus dates the city's ruin from that day.

The Idumeans lived south of Judea in old Edom. In 68 the Zealots called them to Jerusalem, and about 20,000 came (Jewish War 4.4.2). The gates were shut against them, but during a violent storm at night the Zealots sawed through the bars and let them in (Jewish War 4.4.6-7). Josephus says the outer temple court flowed with blood, and about 8,500 died there (Jewish War 4.5.1). They killed Ananus and other priests and left their bodies unburied. Josephus writes that the death of Ananus was the beginning of the city's destruction (Jewish War 4.5.2). The fulfilled reading adds a contrast. If a Jewish writer could see the city's fall flowing from the murder of a high priest, the Gospels see it flowing from the rejection of Jesus, the great High Priest (Luke 21:22; Acts 3:14-15).
Jewish War 4.5.2: "the death of Ananus was the beginning of the destruction of the city".
Some writers suggest the Christians left for Pella around this time. Eusebius only says they left before the war (Church History 3.5.3).

Scholars of all views accept these events as history. Some question whether they are the specific "abomination" Jesus meant. Futurists see them as part of a local judgment that does not exhaust the prophecy. Critics note that Josephus wrote with his own bias against the rebel groups.
Were the Roman legions and their standards the abomination?
This is the most common fulfilled view. The legions surrounded the city, and once the temple burned the soldiers sacrificed to their standards in the temple court.

Roman legions carried standards topped with eagles and images of the emperor. Soldiers gave them religious honour. Jews saw them as idols, so governors normally kept them out of Jerusalem. When Pilate brought images into the city by night, Jews protested so strongly that he removed them (Josephus, Antiquities 18.3.1). In August AD 70, while the temple was still burning, soldiers set up their standards near the eastern gate. They offered sacrifices to them there and hailed Titus as imperator (Jewish War 6.6.1). An idol set up and honoured where God's altar stood fits "abomination". An army that destroys fits "desolation". This view also matches Luke 21:20, where the sign is Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
Jewish War 6.6.1: the Romans brought their standards into the temple and offered sacrifices to them.
Antiquities 18.5.3: the Roman official Vitellius led his army around Judea so that its images would not pass through Jewish land.

Some object that the sacrifice to the standards came after the temple burned, too late to warn anyone to flee. Fulfilled interpreters answer that the armies' approach was the warning, and the sacrifice completed the act. Futurists say the act was not done by one man claiming deity, as 2 Thessalonians 2:4 describes.
Could the temple's own priesthood be the deepest form of the abomination?
Some fulfilled interpreters think so. After Christ's sacrifice, ongoing animal sacrifices by priests who rejected him were, on this view, false worship in God's sight.

This view starts with Ezekiel. In Ezekiel 5:11 God says he will withdraw because his own people defiled his sanctuary. In Ezekiel 8-11 the prophet sees idolatry inside the temple, and then God's glory leaves (Ezekiel 10:18; 11:23). Only after that did Babylon destroy it. In the Gospels Jesus calls the temple a "house of trade" and a "den of robbers" (John 2:16; Matthew 21:13). The chief priests led the call for his death (Matthew 27:20). On this reading, once the true Lamb had died, sacrifices offered by priests who rejected him became an empty and offensive rite. God then left the house "desolate" (Matthew 23:38). John Calvin wrote along similar lines that the temple lost its holiness once the covenant was broken. Outside armies only finished what the inner defilement began.
Ezekiel 10:18 and 11:23: God's glory leaves the temple, and only then does Babylon burn it in 586 BC.
Hebrews 10:11-14: after Christ's one offering, the daily repeated sacrifices can no longer take away sins.

Many scholars, including some who hold the fulfilled view, think this stretches the word "abomination", which in Daniel points to a pagan idol. Futurists hold that the term requires an idol set up by a ruler. Some note that the apostles still worshipped in the temple (Acts 3:1; 21:26), so it was not yet simply false worship.
What does the law of the leprous house (Leviticus 14) have to do with Jesus leaving the temple?
On this reading, Jesus acts like the priest who inspects a diseased house. He goes out, declares it desolate, and foretells that its stones will be torn down.

Leviticus 14:33-47 gives a law for a house with spreading mould. The priest inspects it, goes out of the house, and shuts it up (Leviticus 14:38). If the disease returns, the house is unclean. It must be torn down, and its stones taken outside the city (Leviticus 14:44-45). The fulfilled reading sees a pattern in Jesus' actions. He inspected the temple at the start and at the end of his ministry (John 2:13-17; Matthew 21:12-13). He declared it "desolate" (Matthew 23:38). He "went out" from it (Matthew 24:1). Then he said that not one stone would be left on another (Matthew 24:2). As the great High Priest (Hebrews 5:6), he gives the verdict that the house must come down.
Leviticus 14:38 says the priest "shall go out of the house". Matthew 24:1 says Jesus "went out" from the temple.
In AD 70 the Romans pulled down the temple buildings. Josephus says the city was so leveled that visitors could hardly believe it had been lived in (Jewish War 7.1.1).

Many commentators see this as a creative typology rather than the plain point of the text, since no Gospel quotes Leviticus 14 here. Futurists accept that Jesus judged the temple of his day but still expect a later temple. Most interpreters agree that Matthew 23:38 and 24:2 foretell AD 70.
Is the Antichrist mentioned in Matthew 24?
No. The word "antichrist" does not occur in Matthew 24. It appears only in John's letters, where it describes false teachers already present.

Matthew 24 speaks of false christs and false prophets (Matthew 24:5, 11, 24). It speaks of the abomination of desolation. But it never names a single world ruler called "the Antichrist". The word appears only in 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3 and 2 John 7. There John says "many antichrists have come" and that the spirit of antichrist was "already in the world". He means people who deny that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh. The fulfilled reading says that a future Antichrist in a rebuilt temple is a figure built by joining texts from Daniel, Paul and Revelation. Jesus' own warning is about a sacrilege and a flight, not about a single end-time dictator.
1 John 2:18: "even now many antichrists have arisen" — John's readers already faced them.
Paul's "man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4) is linked to the temple by many interpreters, but Paul does not use the word "antichrist".

Futurists answer that the person who sets up the abomination is the same as Paul's man of lawlessness and John's beast. They hold that John's "antichrists" are forerunners of one final Antichrist. Many in the Reformation identified the Antichrist with the papacy. Amillennial scholars often expect a final opposer at the end of the age.
If the temple was a "copy and shadow", why would God restore it in the future?
On the fulfilled reading, he would not. The cross completed what the temple pictured, and the torn veil showed that its work was finished.

Hebrews calls the priesthood and sanctuary "a copy and shadow of the heavenly things" (Hebrews 8:5). It says the old covenant was "becoming obsolete" and "near to vanishing" (Hebrews 8:13). When Jesus died, the temple veil tore from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51). Jesus had told the Samaritan woman that true worship would no longer be tied to Jerusalem (John 4:21-23). He said, "It is finished" (John 19:30). Nineteenth-century bishop J. C. Ryle wrote that the temple system's work was done at the cross, and its ruin in AD 70 was its solemn burial. On this reading, a rebuilt temple with animal sacrifice would turn believers back to shadows after the reality has come. Christ's body and his people are now God's temple (John 2:21; 1 Corinthians 3:16).
Hebrews 9:8-12 says the way into the holy place was not yet open while the first tent stood.
Hebrews 10:18: where sins are forgiven, "there is no longer any offering for sin".

Dispensationalists expect a millennial temple, based on Ezekiel 40-48. They say its sacrifices will be memorials, or will deal with ritual cleansing, not atonement for sin. Other premillennialists read Ezekiel's temple symbolically. Amillennial and postmillennial scholars generally read Ezekiel 40-48 as a picture of the church or the new creation.
Why do the details about housetops, cloaks, winter and the Sabbath matter?
They show a local event in first-century Judea, where people lived on flat roofs and Sabbath travel was limited. The escape had to be immediate.

Jesus said that a man on the housetop must not go down for his goods, and a man in the field must not go back for his cloak (Matthew 24:17-18). Houses in Judea had flat roofs used for work and rest, often with outside stairs (Deuteronomy 22:8; Joshua 2:6; Acts 10:9). He told them to pray that the flight would not be in winter, when the wadis flood and roads are hard. He also said not on a Sabbath, when travel was limited to a "Sabbath day's journey" of about 2,000 cubits (Acts 1:12). He grieved for pregnant and nursing women (Matthew 24:19). These details picture people running out of one region on foot. The fulfilled reading says they suit Judea before AD 70, not a worldwide crisis. The words also echo Lot's escape from Sodom (Genesis 19:17, 26; Luke 17:31-32).
Luke 17:31-32 joins the same warning about the housetop to "remember Lot's wife".
A Sabbath day's journey was about 2,000 cubits, roughly one kilometre (Acts 1:12).

Futurists answer that these details fit a future Israel in which Jews again keep the Sabbath and live in Judea. They say a future temple and Jewish population would make the details literal again. Other scholars hold that the warning fit AD 70 and also serves as a pattern for the end.
How could people escape from a city surrounded by armies?
In November AD 66 the Roman general Cestius Gallus suddenly withdrew from Jerusalem. This gave believers a window to leave, and early tradition says they fled to Pella.

In autumn AD 66 Cestius Gallus, governor of Syria, marched on Jerusalem and attacked the temple wall. Then, Josephus says, he withdrew "without any reason in the world" (Jewish War 2.19.7). The rebels chased him and defeated his army at Beth-horon. After this, Josephus says, many leading Jews left the city "as from a sinking ship" (Jewish War 2.20.1). The church historian Eusebius writes that the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, left before the war and settled in Pella, a city across the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). The fulfilled reading sees here the exact sign of Luke 21:20-21. The armies came, then a pause opened the door, and those who believed Jesus' words left in time.
Jewish War 2.19.7: Cestius retreats when the city was nearly taken.
Epiphanius (Panarion 29.7) also records that the believers moved to Pella before the siege.

Some modern historians doubt the Pella tradition, since it is recorded only from the fourth century. Others defend it, noting that Eusebius drew on older sources. Futurists accept that some fled in AD 70 but expect a fuller fulfilment when a future Jewish remnant flees, as in Revelation 12:6.
Were the horrors of the siege foretold in Scripture?
Yes. Moses warned that a covenant-breaking people would eat their own children in a siege. Josephus records this in AD 70.

Deuteronomy 28:53-57 warns that if Israel broke the covenant, an enemy would besiege them so tightly that parents would eat their own children. This happened in the Babylonian siege (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10) and in an earlier siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29). Josephus tells of a woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, who did the same thing during the Roman siege (Jewish War 6.3.4). He says famine killed huge numbers. In all, he gives 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 captives (Jewish War 6.9.3). Jesus had warned of this when he wept over the city and said its enemies would "surround you" because it did not know "the time of your visitation" (Luke 19:41-44). This reading sees AD 70 as the covenant curses coming to their full measure.
Jewish War 6.3.4: Mary of Bethezuba's act shocked even hardened soldiers.
Tacitus says 600,000 were in the besieged city (Histories 5.13). Numbers differ, but all sources describe a huge loss of life.

Scholars of all views accept Deuteronomy 28 as covenant curses and AD 70 as a terrible fulfilment. Futurists hold that the curses also look ahead to a final distress before Israel's national restoration. Many historians think Josephus' total is too high for the city's likely population.
Why have prophecy teachers kept saying the great tribulation is about to begin?
Because they place Matthew 24's signs in our future and then read each new crisis as one of them. The same claim has been made in every decade.

In April 1975 Jack Van Impe's newsletter asked whether the Messiah would come in 1975 and the tribulation in 1976. In 1977 Salem Kirban said the prophetic clock stood at "11:59" and pointed to Iran under the Shah. In 1980 Hal Lindsey said the 1980s could be history's last decade. In January 1991, during the Gulf War, John Walvoord told a newspaper that the prophecy clock was ticking. Each claim rested on reading Matthew 24 as a list of signs for the end of our age. The fulfilled reading says this is the root error. Jesus gave those signs to his own disciples and set their limit: "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). When the signs are moved out of the first century, any war or earthquake can be made to fit.
Kirban's 1977 book made Iran a leading end-time power. Two years later the Shah fell and the scenario changed.
Lindsey's 1970 book said the Antichrist was alive then. More than fifty years later that claim has not been shown true.

Most futurist scholars reject date setting and admit that some popular teachers went too far. They hold that the signs of Matthew 24 are real, that they will grow stronger before Christ returns, and that watchfulness is commanded (Matthew 24:42). They say failed predictions misuse prophecy but do not disprove a future tribulation.
Do the signs in Matthew 24:4-14 describe our age or the years before AD 70?
On the fulfilled reading, they describe the forty years between Jesus' words and the fall of Jerusalem. Acts and Josephus record each of them.

Walvoord listed nine features from Matthew 24:4-14: false christs, wars and rumours of wars, famines, plagues, earthquakes, martyrs, false prophets, growing wickedness, and the gospel preached to the nations. He took these as marks of the whole church age. The fulfilled reading notes that Jesus gave them as answers to the disciples' question about the temple (Matthew 24:2-3). He addressed them as "you": "they will deliver you up" (Matthew 24:9). Each sign can be found before AD 70. There was a famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28). There were earthquakes, such as at Laodicea about AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). Apostles were martyred. Paul said the gospel had gone to "all creation under heaven" (Colossians 1:23). The limit was "this generation" (Matthew 24:34).
Acts 11:28: Agabus foretells a great famine, which came "in the days of Claudius" (AD 41-54).
Romans 1:8 and Colossians 1:6 speak of the gospel already known "in all the world".

Futurists say these signs are general and recur through history, but will grow sharper at the end like birth pains. Many amillennial scholars see them as marks of the whole age between Christ's comings. Some evangelical scholars hold that verses 4-14 fit both the first century and the time before Christ's return.
Should prophecy teachers be held accountable for failed predictions?
Scripture says a word that does not come true was not spoken by the Lord. Teachers who give confident timelines should own their errors.

Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gives a simple test. If a prophet speaks in the Lord's name and the thing does not happen, the Lord did not speak it. Popular teachers often protect themselves by saying "no one knows the day or the hour" and then still say the end is "soon, perhaps tonight". A 1991 newspaper column joked that buyers of end-time timelines should demand a money-back guarantee. The fulfilled reading makes a more serious point. Repeated failures harm the church's witness and make the Bible look unreliable (2 Peter 3:3-4). They also draw believers away from present duties. The answer is not to give up prophecy but to read it as Jesus framed it, with its own time markers. Humble teachers should say plainly when they were wrong (James 3:1).
